sources.title: Women: was your autoimmune condition misdiagnosed?
Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS
Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

en.title: Women More Likely to Receive Psychiatric Misdiagnoses for Autoimmune Conditions
en.dek: Research shows women wait longer for autoimmune diagnoses and are more often misdiagnosed with psychiatric conditions.
facts: Women are 43% more likely than men to receive a psychiatric misdiagnosis for autoimmune conditions, according to a study by Cambridge University and the University of East Anglia (S1).
Women are 74% more likely to receive a psychosomatic misdiagnosis for autoimmune conditions (S1).
Women report delays of one to two years before diagnosis, compared to less than three months for men (S1).
A 2024 systematic review found around 15% of people diagnosed with multiple sclerosis may have another condition, with females twice as likely to be misdiagnosed (S2).
An international survey of 6,607 participants found women experience longer diagnostic delays than men (S3).
body: Autoimmune diseases affect roughly one in ten people globally, The Guardian reports (S1). A new study from Cambridge University and the University of East Anglia found a stark gender divide in diagnosis patterns (S1).

Women are 43% more likely than men to receive a psychiatric misdiagnosis, meaning an autoimmune issue is mistaken for a mental health problem (S1). They are also 74% more likely to receive a psychosomatic misdiagnosis, where symptoms are considered psychological or stress‑induced (S1).
The same study reported that women experience longer periods between symptom onset and diagnosis, with delays of one to two years, whereas men receive a diagnosis in less than three months (S1).

A 2024 systematic review and meta‑analysis indicated that about 15% of people diagnosed with multiple sclerosis may actually have another condition, and females are twice as likely to be misdiagnosed (S2). Misdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary treatments and emotional distress, a neurologist told Healthline (S2).
An international survey published in eClinicalMedicine, involving 6,607 participants, also found women experience longer diagnostic delays than men (S3).
en.context: Autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system attacks the body’s own cells, affect an estimated 4.6% of the U.S. population (S3). Misdiagnosis can delay proper treatment and expose patients to unnecessary medication and anxiety (S2, S3).

problemsFixed: First sentence attributes global prevalence statistic to the study, but the study concerns gender divide; prevalence is a separate statement in the Guardian article.
Use of 'averaging one to two years' implies a calculated mean; source gives a range ('one to two years').
MS misdiagnosis rate stated as 'actually have another condition' without 'may', overstating certainty; source says 'may actually have another condition'.
Context's second sentence synthesizes implications without direct attribution; should attribute to sources.
